warmup.q: spent is an AtomicLong. Eight request threads run if (spent.get() + cents <= limit) spent.addAndGet(cents);. Can the card go over its limit?
options: No, but only because addAndGet is atomic
Yes: two threads can both pass the check before either adds
Yes, but only on ARM processors
warmup.why: Each call is atomic on its own. The check and the add are two calls, with a gap between them, so two threads can both see room for one more payment and both add. This is check-then-act from lesson 3, built out of atomic parts. The fix is to do the check inside one compare-and-set, which this lesson shows.

sections.h: An atomic variable does read-modify-write in one step
sections.html:
Lesson 3 of this track promised to show how AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() fixes count++. Start with what you get:

Java
private final AtomicLong authorized = new AtomicLong();   // no lock needed

void onApproved(long cents) {
    authorized.addAndGet(cents);          // read, add, write: one indivisible step
}

long total() {
    return authorized.get();              // a volatile read: sees the latest value
}
Kotlin
private val authorized = AtomicLong()      // no lock needed

fun onApproved(cents: Long) {
    authorized.addAndGet(cents)            // read, add, write: one indivisible step
}

fun total(): Long = authorized.get()       // a volatile read: sees the latest value

An atomic variable holds one value and offers read-modify-write operations that no other thread can split. addAndGet reads, adds and writes as one step. Its get() and set() behave like reads and writes of a volatile field, so every thread sees the latest value.

The method names tell you what comes back. incrementAndGet() returns the new value and getAndIncrement() the old one. The same pairs exist for add, update and accumulate. AtomicInteger, AtomicLong, AtomicBoolean and AtomicReference cover most needs, and AtomicIntegerArray and AtomicLongArray give you arrays of them.

How does a library turn three steps into one without a lock? The CPU has instructions for it. On x86, HotSpot compiles getAndAdd to a single lock xadd instruction and compareAndSet to lock cmpxchg, and ARM64 has its own equivalents. While the instruction runs, the core keeps the variable's cache line to itself, so no other core can get in between the read and the write.

No thread ever waits for another. If the scheduler pauses a thread, it is never in the middle of an atomic update: the instruction either happened or it didn't. So some thread always makes progress, which is what lock-free means. Compare that with a lock: a thread that is paused while holding it stops every thread that needs it.

Atomics have one hard limit. Each one protects exactly one variable. Two atomics are not atomic together, and neither are two calls on the same atomic, as the warm-up showed.

Predict from the mechanism. The operating system pauses thread A for 50 ms. With an AtomicLong, what do the other request threads do during those 50 ms? And with a lock that A held at that moment? (With the atomic, they keep updating: A was paused before or after its instruction, never inside it. With the lock, every thread that needs it waits the full 50 ms.)

sections.h: Compare-and-set is the primitive, and the loop is the pattern
sections.html:
Almost every atomic operation is built on compare-and-set (CAS). compareAndSet(expected, next) does this as one step: if the current value equals expected, store next and return true; otherwise change nothing and return false.

That is enough to build any read-modify-write, with a loop. Here is the lab's max tracker:

Java
long prev;
do {
    prev = max.get();                       // 1. read
    if (amount <= prev) return;             // 2. decide: nothing to do
} while (!max.compareAndSet(prev, amount)); // 3. write only if max is still prev; else retry
Kotlin
var prev: Long
do {
    prev = max.get()                        // 1. read
    if (amount <= prev) return              // 2. decide: nothing to do
} while (!max.compareAndSet(prev, amount))  // 3. write only if max is still prev; else retry

Read the value. Decide what the new value should be. Then store it, but only if nobody changed the value since you read it. If someone did, your decision was based on old data, so throw it away and start again. The figure shows two threads that both read 41. T1's CAS wins. T2's fails, so T2 reads 42 and writes 43. Nothing is lost.

Compare that with the broken tracker in the lab, if (amount > max) max = amount on a volatile field. It reads, decides, and then writes blindly, whatever happened in between. CAS turns the blind write into a conditional one.

A failed CAS costs a retry, not a wait. With little contention, retries are rare. With many threads hammering one variable, threads keep failing and re-reading, and the variable's cache line bounces from core to core. The section on LongAdder deals with that cost.

try.title: Watch CAS fail and retry
steps: Read CasRetries. Its increment() is a hand-written CAS loop that counts its own failures.
Predict the failure count for 1 thread, then for 8 threads.
Run it twice. Check that counter is always exact.

code.title: CasRetries.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l08; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; /** A hand-written compare-and-set increment. Count how often the CAS fails as threads are added. */ public class CasRetries { static final AtomicLong counter = new AtomicLong(); // returns how many times compareAndSet failed before it worked static long increment() { long failures = 0; while (true) { long seen = counter.get(); // 1. read if (counter.compareAndSet(seen, seen + 1)) { // 2. write only if still `seen` return failures; } failures++; // 3. someone else won: retry } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { int perThread = 1_000_000; for (int threads : new int[] {1, 2, 4, 8}) { counter.set(0); AtomicLong failed = new AtomicLong(); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); // start them all together List<Thread> ts = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < threads; i++) { ts.add(new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } long mine = 0; for (int n = 0; n < perThread; n++) mine += increment(); failed.addAndGet(mine); })); } for (Thread t : ts) t.start(); go.countDown(); for (Thread t : ts) t.join(); System.out.printf("threads: %d counter: %,10d failed CAS: %,10d (%.2f per increment)%n", threads, counter.get(), failed.get(), failed.get() / (double) counter.get()); } } }

alt.title: CasRetries.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l08 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong import kotlin.concurrent.thread // A hand-written compare-and-set increment. Count how often the CAS fails as threads are added. private val counter = AtomicLong() // returns how many times compareAndSet failed before it worked private fun increment(): Long { var failures = 0L while (true) { val seen = counter.get() // 1. read if (counter.compareAndSet(seen, seen + 1)) { // 2. write only if still `seen` return failures } failures++ // 3. someone else won: retry } } fun main() { val perThread = 1_000_000 for (threads in listOf(1, 2, 4, 8)) { counter.set(0) val failed = AtomicLong() val go = CountDownLatch(1) // start them all together val ts = List(threads) { thread { go.await() var mine = 0L repeat(perThread) { mine += increment() } failed.addAndGet(mine) } } go.countDown() ts.forEach { it.join() } println("threads: %d counter: %,10d failed CAS: %,10d (%.2f per increment)" .format(threads, counter.get(), failed.get(), failed.get() / counter.get().toDouble())) } }

try.expect: One thread never fails: nobody else changes the value. With more threads, failures climb into the tens of thousands or millions, and the number changes a lot from run to run. The counter is exact every time. Failures stay below one per increment here, because a core tends to get a run of increments done before another core takes the cache line away.

video.title: Two threads read 41, one compare-and-set wins, the other fails, reads 42 and retries

sections.h: The update methods write the loop for you, and may run your function twice
sections.html:
You rarely need to write the loop yourself. updateAndGet(f) and accumulateAndGet(x, f) contain it:

Java
max.accumulateAndGet(amount, Math::max);          // the same loop, written for you
balance.updateAndGet(b -> b + 100);               // any pure function of the old value
Kotlin
max.accumulateAndGet(amount, Math::max)           // the same loop, written for you
balance.updateAndGet { b -> b + 100 }             // any pure function of the old value

Inside, they read the value, call your function, and CAS. When the CAS fails, they call your function again with the new value. So your function can run more than once for one update, and some of its results are thrown away.

That means the function must be a pure function of its input. No logging, no counters, no calls to other services, no reads of other shared state that might change. updateAndGet(b -> { audit.log(b); return b - cents; }) can log balances that the account never had. Do side effects after the call returns, using the value it returned.

The get variants, getAndUpdate and getAndAccumulate, return the value from before the update. Use them when the caller needs to know whether its own update applied. The worked example uses exactly that to build a spend limit.

try.title: Count the calls
steps: Read UpdateTwice. Four threads make 250,000 deposits each with updateAndGet, and the function counts how often it runs.
Predict: will the function run exactly 1,000,000 times?
Run it two or three times.

code.title: UpdateTwice.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l08; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder; /** updateAndGet retries your function when it loses a race. Count how often the function really runs. */ public class UpdateTwice { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { AtomicLong balance = new AtomicLong(); LongAdder calls = new LongAdder(); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); Runnable deposits = () -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } for (int i = 0; i < 250_000; i++) { balance.updateAndGet(b -> { calls.increment(); // a side effect: imagine this sent a notification return b + 1; }); } }; Thread[] ts = {new Thread(deposits), new Thread(deposits), new Thread(deposits), new Thread(deposits)}; for (Thread t : ts) t.start(); go.countDown(); // all four start together for (Thread t : ts) t.join(); System.out.printf("updates: %,d times the function ran: %,d%n", balance.get(), calls.sum()); } }

alt.title: UpdateTwice.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l08 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder import kotlin.concurrent.thread // updateAndGet retries your function when it loses a race. Count how often the function really runs. fun main() { val balance = AtomicLong() val calls = LongAdder() val go = CountDownLatch(1) val ts = List(4) { thread { go.await() repeat(250_000) { balance.updateAndGet { b -> calls.increment() // a side effect: imagine this sent a notification b + 1 } } } } go.countDown() // all four start together ts.forEach { it.join() } println("updates: %,d times the function ran: %,d".format(balance.get(), calls.sum())) }

try.expect: The balance is exactly 1,000,000 every time. The function runs more often than that, a few percent more in runs here (for example 1,026,201 times). Each extra call is a lost CAS race whose result was thrown away. If that function had sent a notification, customers would have received tens of thousands of duplicates.

sections.h: LongAdder for hot counters, AtomicLong for decisions
sections.html:
A single AtomicLong that sixteen threads increment is one cache line that every core wants at the same moment. Each increment has to pull the line over to its core, and the cores spend their time passing it around.

LongAdder (JDK 8) spreads the count over several cells. When threads collide, it moves them to different cells, so they mostly write to different cache lines. sum() adds the base value and all the cells together.

Java
private final LongAdder declines = new LongAdder();

void onDecline() { declines.increment(); }        // threads mostly hit different cells
long declinesSoFar() { return declines.sum(); }   // adds the cells up: not a snapshot
Kotlin
private val declines = LongAdder()

fun onDecline() = declines.increment()             // threads mostly hit different cells
fun declinesSoFar(): Long = declines.sum()         // adds the cells up: not a snapshot

The price is in sum(). It reads the cells one by one while other threads keep adding, and its Javadoc says plainly that the result is not an atomic snapshot: increments that happen during the sum might not be counted. The adder also uses more memory than one long.

That gives a clean rule. Use LongAdder for statistics that many threads update and someone reads now and then: requests served, declines, records consumed. Use AtomicLong when the value drives a decision, such as a spend limit, a sequence number or a rate limit. There you need the exact current value and a compare-and-set against it, and LongAdder has neither. LongAccumulator does the same trick for any associative function, such as max, with the same caveat on reads.

try.title: Race an AtomicLong against a LongAdder
steps: Read AdderVsAtomic: 8 threads each count 2,000,000 events, first on one AtomicLong, then on a LongAdder.
Predict which is faster, and by roughly how much.
Run it. Then change the thread count in time to 1 and run it again.

code.title: AdderVsAtomic.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l08; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder; /** 8 threads each count 2,000,000 events: once on one AtomicLong, once on a LongAdder. */ public class AdderVsAtomic { static long time(Runnable perThreadWork) throws InterruptedException { Thread[] ts = new Thread[8]; for (int i = 0; i < ts.length; i++) ts[i] = new Thread(perThreadWork); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (Thread t : ts) t.start(); for (Thread t : ts) t.join(); return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { int n = 2_000_000; for (int round = 1; round <= 3; round++) { AtomicLong atomic = new AtomicLong(); LongAdder adder = new LongAdder(); long a = time(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) atomic.incrementAndGet(); }); long b = time(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) adder.increment(); }); System.out.printf("round %d: AtomicLong %,d in %4d ms LongAdder %,d in %4d ms%n", round, atomic.get(), a, adder.sum(), b); } } }

alt.title: AdderVsAtomic.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l08 import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder import kotlin.concurrent.thread // 8 threads each count 2,000,000 events: once on one AtomicLong, once on a LongAdder. private fun time(perThreadWork: () -> Unit): Long { val t0 = System.nanoTime() List(8) { thread { perThreadWork() } }.forEach { it.join() } return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 } fun main() { val n = 2_000_000 for (round in 1..3) { val atomic = AtomicLong() val adder = LongAdder() val a = time { repeat(n) { atomic.incrementAndGet() } } val b = time { repeat(n) { adder.increment() } } println("round %d: AtomicLong %,d in %4d ms LongAdder %,d in %4d ms".format(round, atomic.get(), a, adder.sum(), b)) } }

try.expect: Both totals are exactly 16,000,000. With 8 threads, the LongAdder was 4 to 10 times faster in runs here (for example 400 ms against 66 ms). With 1 thread the gap shrinks or disappears, because there is no contention for the adder to avoid.

sections.h: AtomicReference swaps a whole object at once
sections.html:
AtomicReference<V> does compare-and-set on a reference. Combine it with an immutable object and you can change several fields as one step: build a new object from the old one, then swap the reference.

Java
record Breaker(State state, int failures, Instant openedAt) {}   // immutable

private final AtomicReference<Breaker> breaker =
        new AtomicReference<>(new Breaker(State.CLOSED, 0, null));

void onFailure(Instant now) {
    breaker.updateAndGet(b -> b.failures() + 1 >= 5
            ? new Breaker(State.OPEN, b.failures() + 1, now)          // trip
            : new Breaker(b.state(), b.failures() + 1, b.openedAt()));
}
Kotlin
data class Breaker(val state: State, val failures: Int, val openedAt: Instant?)   // immutable

private val breaker = AtomicReference(Breaker(State.CLOSED, 0, null))

fun onFailure(now: Instant) {
    breaker.updateAndGet { b ->
        if (b.failures + 1 >= 5) Breaker(State.OPEN, b.failures + 1, now)   // trip
        else b.copy(failures = b.failures + 1)
    }
}

The CAS compares references with ==, not equals. That is what you want here, because every update builds a new object.

The lab's Treiber stack uses the same idea on a linked list. A node never changes after it is built. To push, build a node that points at the current head, then CAS the head from that old head to the new node:

Java
void push(T item) {
    Node<T> top, node;
    do {
        top = head.get();
        node = new Node<>(item, top);           // build the new node off to the side
    } while (!head.compareAndSet(top, node));   // publish it only if head is still top
}
Kotlin
fun push(item: T) {
    var top: Node<T>?
    var node: Node<T>
    do {
        top = head.get()
        node = Node(item, top)                  // build the new node off to the side
    } while (!head.compareAndSet(top, node))    // publish it only if head is still top
}

CAS has one blind spot, called ABA. It checks that the value is the same as when you read it, not that it never changed. If the head goes from node A to B and back to A while your thread is paused, your CAS succeeds, although the list behind A is now different.

In Java, ABA needs reuse: a node pool, recycled objects, array indices or plain numbers. With freshly allocated nodes, the garbage collector never reuses A's memory while your thread still holds a reference to A, so the lab's stack is safe. When you do recycle, AtomicStampedReference pairs the reference with an int stamp that you bump on every change, so A with stamp 0 and A with stamp 3 no longer match.

try.title: Play out ABA by hand
steps: Read AbaDemo. It plays two threads on one thread, step by step, so the bad interleaving happens every time. Nodes are recycled.
Before you run it, predict the stack after T1's compareAndSet.
Run it and compare the plain AtomicReference with the AtomicStampedReference.

code.title: AbaDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l08; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicStampedReference; /** * The ABA problem, played out by hand on one thread so it happens every time. * Nodes are recycled (mutable next), as in a pooled or off-heap structure. */ public class AbaDemo { static final class Node { final String name; Node next; Node(String name, Node next) { this.name = name; this.next = next; } } static String show(Node n) { StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); for (; n != null; n = n.next) sb.append(n.name).append(n.next != null ? " -> " : ""); return sb.length() == 0 ? "(empty)" : sb.toString(); } public static void main(String[] args) { Node c = new Node("C", null), b = new Node("B", c), a = new Node("A", b); AtomicReference<Node> head = new AtomicReference<>(a); System.out.println("start: " + show(head.get())); Node top = head.get(), next = top.next; // T1 starts a pop... System.out.println("T1 reads top=A, next=B, then is paused"); head.set(b); // T2 pops A head.set(c); // T2 pops B (B is now T2's) a.next = head.get(); head.set(a); // T2 pushes the recycled A System.out.println("T2 pops A, pops B, pushes A again: " + show(head.get())); boolean ok = head.compareAndSet(top, next); // T1 resumes: head is A again System.out.println("T1 resumes: compareAndSet(A, B) = " + ok); System.out.println("stack now: " + show(head.get()) + " (B was popped by T2: corrupted)"); System.out.println(); a.next = b; b.next = c; AtomicStampedReference<Node> stamped = new AtomicStampedReference<>(a, 0); int[] stampHolder = new int[1]; Node top2 = stamped.get(stampHolder); // T1 reads the node AND the stamp int stamp = stampHolder[0]; Node next2 = top2.next; System.out.println("T1 reads top=A, stamp=" + stamp + ", next=B, then is paused"); stamped.set(b, 1); // every change bumps the stamp stamped.set(c, 2); a.next = c; stamped.set(a, 3); System.out.println("T2 pops A, pops B, pushes A again: stamp is now " + stamped.getStamp()); boolean ok2 = stamped.compareAndSet(top2, next2, stamp, stamp + 1); System.out.println("T1 resumes: compareAndSet(A, B, stamp " + stamp + ") = " + ok2 + ", so T1 re-reads and retries"); } }

alt.title: AbaDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l08 import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicStampedReference // The ABA problem, played out by hand on one thread so it happens every time. // Nodes are recycled (mutable next), as in a pooled or off-heap structure. private class AbaNode(val name: String, var next: AbaNode?) private fun show(start: AbaNode?): String = generateSequence(start) { it.next }.joinToString(" -> ") { it.name }.ifEmpty { "(empty)" } fun main() { val c = AbaNode("C", null) val b = AbaNode("B", c) val a = AbaNode("A", b) val head = AtomicReference(a) println("start: ${show(head.get())}") val top = head.get() val next = top.next // T1 starts a pop... println("T1 reads top=A, next=B, then is paused") head.set(b) // T2 pops A head.set(c) // T2 pops B (B is now T2's) a.next = head.get() head.set(a) // T2 pushes the recycled A println("T2 pops A, pops B, pushes A again: ${show(head.get())}") val ok = head.compareAndSet(top, next) // T1 resumes: head is A again println("T1 resumes: compareAndSet(A, B) = $ok") println("stack now: ${show(head.get())} (B was popped by T2: corrupted)") println() a.next = b; b.next = c val stamped = AtomicStampedReference(a, 0) val stampHolder = IntArray(1) val top2 = stamped.get(stampHolder) // T1 reads the node AND the stamp val stamp = stampHolder[0] val next2 = top2.next println("T1 reads top=A, stamp=$stamp, next=B, then is paused") stamped.set(b, 1) // every change bumps the stamp stamped.set(c, 2) a.next = c stamped.set(a, 3) println("T2 pops A, pops B, pushes A again: stamp is now ${stamped.stamp}") val ok2 = stamped.compareAndSet(top2, next2, stamp, stamp + 1) println("T1 resumes: compareAndSet(A, B, stamp $stamp) = $ok2, so T1 re-reads and retries") }

try.expect: With the plain reference, T1's compareAndSet(A, B) returns true and the stack becomes B -> C, although T2 had already popped B: the stack is corrupted. With the stamp, the same CAS returns false, because the stamp moved from 0 to 3, so T1 re-reads and retries.

analogy: Compare-and-set is a git push that only succeeds if the remote is still at the commit you started from. If a teammate pushed first, yours is rejected; you pull, rebase your change onto theirs, and push again. Nobody locks the repository, and nobody's commit is lost. ABA is the remote going from commit X to Y and then being force-pushed back to X: your check passes, though history changed underneath you. A version stamp on the branch fixes that. The analogy breaks on cost: a rejected push costs you minutes, while a failed CAS costs nanoseconds, so a thread just tries again at once.
world: In a Kafka consumer with 12 partitions on 12 threads, a records-processed counter is a LongAdder, and the highest offset seen for a lag gauge is an AtomicLong with accumulateAndGet(offset, Math::max). A circuit breaker around the 120 ms card-issuer API keeps its state in an AtomicReference to an immutable record, as in the last section. A "close once" guard is closed.compareAndSet(false, true) on an AtomicBoolean. The spend limit in the worked example is correct inside one JVM. Across several pods it belongs in the database, and the shape is the same: UPDATE card SET spent = spent + ? WHERE id = ? AND spent + ? <= daily_limit, then check that one row changed. That is a compare-and-set in SQL.
mistake: The most common mistake is building check-then-act out of atomic calls: if (counter.get() < limit) counter.incrementAndGet(). Each call is atomic and the pair is not, which is lesson 3's bug one level down. The second form is two atomics that must change together, such as count and totalCents for an average: a reader can see the new count with the old total. People make these mistakes because "I used AtomicLong" feels like "this is thread-safe". The fix is one compare-and-set that includes the check (a CAS loop, updateAndGet or getAndUpdate), and for several fields, one AtomicReference to an immutable record, or a lock.

compare.title: A max tracker with Java's atomics and Kotlin's

java.title: Java (java.util.concurrent.atomic)
java.html: class MaxTracker { private final AtomicLong max = new AtomicLong(Long.MIN_VALUE); void offer(long amount) { max.accumulateAndGet(amount, Math::max); // CAS loop inside } long max() { return max.get(); } }

kotlin.title: Kotlin (kotlin.concurrent.atomics)
kotlin.html: @OptIn(ExperimentalAtomicApi::class) class MaxTracker { private val max = AtomicLong(Long.MIN_VALUE) // kotlin.concurrent.atomics, not java.util fun offer(amount: Long) { max.update { prev -> maxOf(prev, amount) } // a CAS loop inside, like updateAndGet } fun max(): Long = max.load() }

compare.note: On the JVM most Kotlin code simply uses java.util.concurrent.atomic, and everything in this lesson works the same. Kotlin 2.1 added its own atomics in kotlin.concurrent.atomics, mainly for multiplatform code. The names differ (load, fetchAndAdd, update) and, as of Kotlin 2.4, they still need @OptIn(ExperimentalAtomicApi::class). The behavior is the same compare-and-set underneath. One thing does not change between the languages: @Volatile var count = 0 followed by count++ compiles happily in Kotlin and loses updates exactly like the Java version.

worked.title: A daily spend limit without a lock

steps.say: A card has a daily limit. tryAuthorize must approve only if the new total stays within it, and many request threads call it. Here is a first attempt with an AtomicLong. Look for the race before reading on.
steps.code: private final AtomicLong spent = new AtomicLong(); boolean tryAuthorize(long cents) { if (spent.get() + cents <= limit) { // check spent.addAndGet(cents); // act return true; } return false; }

alt.html: private val spent = AtomicLong() fun tryAuthorize(cents: Long): Boolean { if (spent.get() + cents <= limit) { // check spent.addAndGet(cents) // act return true } return false }

steps.say: Each call on spent is atomic. The pair is not: with 90 of 100 spent, two threads can both pass the check for 10 and both add, ending at 110. Making the variable atomic did not make the logic atomic. The check has to happen inside the compare-and-set.
The CAS loop does the check on the value it is about to replace. If another thread changes spent in between, the CAS fails and the loop decides again on fresh data.
steps.code: boolean tryAuthorize(long cents) { while (true) { long before = spent.get(); // 1. read the current spend if (before + cents > limit) return false; // 2. decide on that value if (spent.compareAndSet(before, before + cents)) return true; // 3. commit, if unchanged } // 4. lost the race: re-read, decide again }

alt.html: fun tryAuthorize(cents: Long): Boolean { while (true) { val before = spent.get() // 1. read the current spend if (before + cents > limit) return false // 2. decide on that value if (spent.compareAndSet(before, before + cents)) return true // 3. commit, if unchanged } // 4. lost the race: re-read, decide again }

steps.say: The same thing with getAndUpdate. The function is pure: it looks only at s. Before reading the next step, explain to yourself why the second line compares before + cents with the limit, instead of checking whether the value changed.
steps.code: boolean tryAuthorize(long cents) { long before = spent.getAndUpdate(s -> s + cents <= limit ? s + cents : s); return before + cents <= limit; // did OUR update apply? }

alt.html: fun tryAuthorize(cents: Long): Boolean { val before = spent.getAndUpdate { s -> if (s + cents <= limit) s + cents else s } return before + cents <= limit // did OUR update apply? }

steps.say: getAndUpdate returns the value that its final, successful call of the function saw. If that value plus cents fits the limit, the function added cents, so this caller is approved. If it didn't fit, the function returned s unchanged and nothing was spent. Checking whether the value changed tells you nothing, because other threads change it all the time. And this is why LongAdder is the wrong tool for a limit: it has no compare-and-set, and its sum() isn't exact while others add.

lab.title: A lock-free max tracker and a Treiber stack
steps: Run the tests. MaxTracker passes the single-thread test and fails the 8-thread one: several raises started from the same old max, which means two threads both replaced it and one update was lost. The three stack tests fail with UnsupportedOperationException.
Fix MaxTracker without synchronized or locks. Replace the volatile long with an AtomicLong and write the CAS loop from the second section. offer still returns the max from before your update.
Write TreiberStack.push: read the head, build a new Node that points at it, compareAndSet the head, and retry on failure. Reject null with a NullPointerException.
Write pop and isEmpty. pop returns null on an empty stack.
Run the tests until all five pass, then twice more.
hints: The loop in offer has two exits, and both return prev: when amount <= prev (no write needed) and when the CAS succeeds.
getAndAccumulate(amount, Math::max) is a one-line answer for offer. Write the loop first, then compare.
In pop, take next from the node you read (top.next), never from a second head.get(). The head may have moved since.
lab.done: All five tests in AtomicsTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: A CAS loop from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write tryTake(AtomicInteger tokens): take one token if any are left and return true, or return false when none are left. Use a compareAndSet loop, no locks. Check: can the count ever go below zero?

answer.html: static boolean tryTake(AtomicInteger tokens) { while (true) { int left = tokens.get(); if (left == 0) return false; // nothing left: no write if (tokens.compareAndSet(left, left - 1)) return true; } // someone else took one: retry }

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: fun tryTake(tokens: AtomicInteger): Boolean { while (true) { val left = tokens.get() if (left == 0) return false // nothing left: no write if (tokens.compareAndSet(left, left - 1)) return true } // someone else took one: retry }

recap: An atomic variable does one read-modify-write as a single step, with volatile visibility, and no thread ever waits for another.
compareAndSet(expected, next) writes only if the value is still expected. Read, decide, CAS, and retry on failure: that loop builds any update.
updateAndGet and friends contain the loop, so your function may run more than once. Keep it pure.
LongAdder beats AtomicLong for hot counters, but sum() is not a snapshot. Use AtomicLong when the value drives a decision.
AtomicReference plus an immutable object updates several fields at once. ABA needs reuse; AtomicStampedReference fixes it.
Two atomic calls in a row are not atomic. Put the check inside the CAS.

explain.prompt: Explain, in your own words, how a compare-and-set loop can update a shared value correctly without any thread ever waiting for a lock.
explain.answer: Each thread reads the current value, computes the value it wants, and then asks the CPU to store it only if the variable still holds what it read. That compare-and-set is a single hardware instruction, so no other thread can slip in between the compare and the store. If another thread changed the value first, the CAS fails and nothing is written, so the thread reads again and recomputes from the fresh value. A thread never waits for another; it just retries. Every failed CAS means some other thread succeeded, so the system as a whole always makes progress. The catch is that the computation may run several times, so it must have no side effects.

deeper.html:
An AtomicLong is a separate object. If you have a million Account objects that each need an atomic counter, that's a million extra objects, each with its own header. The JDK's own classes avoid this by putting a volatile long field in the class and doing CAS on the field in place. Two tools do that. AtomicLongFieldUpdater (and its Integer and Reference siblings) is the older one. VarHandle, since JDK 9, is the general one:

Java
private volatile long spent;
private static final VarHandle SPENT;
static {
    try {
        SPENT = MethodHandles.lookup().findVarHandle(Account.class, "spent", long.class);
    } catch (ReflectiveOperationException e) {
        throw new ExceptionInInitializerError(e);
    }
}

boolean add(long expected, long next) {
    return SPENT.compareAndSet(this, expected, next);   // CAS on this object's field
}
Kotlin
class Account {
    @Volatile private var spent = 0L

    fun add(expected: Long, next: Long): Boolean =
        SPENT.compareAndSet(this, expected, next)        // CAS on this object's field

    companion object {
        private val SPENT: VarHandle = MethodHandles.privateLookupIn(Account::class.java, MethodHandles.lookup())
            .findVarHandle(Account::class.java, "spent", Long::class.java)
    }
}

VarHandle also offers weaker memory orderings (getAcquire, setRelease, plain and opaque access), which the memory model track covers in its last lesson.

Two more details. The weakCompareAndSet family may fail even when the value matches. Inside a retry loop that doesn't matter, and on some ARM processors it can be cheaper. And a CAS loop is lock-free but not wait-free: one unlucky thread could, in theory, lose every race forever while others succeed. In practice that almost never happens, but it is why a hot CAS loop under extreme contention can be slower than a lock, which queues threads instead of letting them all retry at once. LongAdder exists because of exactly that case.
